title: Carl Lewis, King of Sprint and Long Jump
author: adrien-martinot
subject: histoire

blocks.text: Frederick Carlton Lewis was born on July 1, 1961, in Birmingham, Alabama, and grew up in Willingboro, New Jersey. Athletics ran in the family: his parents, Bill and Evelyn, coached a local track club, and his mother had competed as a hurdler at the 1951 Pan American Games. As a boy, Carl was small for his age. Then he grew several centimeters in a single summer, and his results took off.

blocks.text: At the University of Houston, he trained with coach Tom Tellez, who rebuilt his technique in both the sprint and the [[Long jump]]. By 1980 he had earned a place on the US Olympic team, but he never went to Moscow: the United States led the [[1980 Olympic boycott]]. He would have to wait four more years.
His younger sister, Carol Lewis, was also an elite long jumper. She competed at the 1984 Olympics in Los Angeles, the same Games that made her brother famous.

In 1983, at the first World Championships in Helsinki, Lewis won three titles. A year later, in Los Angeles, he matched what [[Jesse Owens]] had done in 1936: four gold medals, in the 100 m, the 200 m, the long jump and the [[4x100 m relay]]. Yet part of the home crowd booed him. After taking an early lead in the long jump, he skipped his last attempts to save his legs, and many found him distant and too sure of himself.

description: Nine Olympic gold medals, four of them in the same event across twelve years. Carl Lewis ran like a sprinter, flew like a jumper and was named athlete of the century. His story also runs through a boycott, a doping scandal and one of the greatest duels in athletics.
